lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Excretion removes waste products from the body; if toxic wastes accumulate, they may cause damage.
  • A neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system and transmits nerve impulses.
  • The skin is an excretory organ because sweat leaves the body through the skin and carries waste materials out with it.
  • Receptors detect stimuli, while effectors such as muscles and glands produce responses.
  • The central nervous system comprises the brain and the spinal cord and acts as the control centre of the nervous system.
  • In the kidneys, blood is filtered at the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule, and urine passes through the ureter to the urinary bladder and out through the urethra.
  • Lithotripsy breaks kidney stones with shock waves, while dialysis cleans blood artificially with a machine called a dialyzer.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Define: excretion.

Ans: Excretion is the process of removing the waste products from the body. Cells produce nitrogenous materials, salts and carbon dioxide as by-products of the metabolic breakdown of sugars, fats and proteins, and if these toxic wastes accumulate in the body they may cause damage. The organ system responsible for this removal is called the excretory system, which removes non-solid wastes through sweat, urine and exhalation.

Q: 2. Define: reflex action.

Ans: An immediate and involuntary response to a stimulus is called a reflex action. These are the sudden, automatic responses of the body which are shown for certain stimuli without the will of the person. For example, the hand is pulled back quickly just after touching a hot object.

Q: 3. Define: neuron.

Ans: A neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system. All parts of the nervous system, i.e. the brain, spinal cord and nerves, are made up of neurons. A neuron consists of two parts, the cell body and the axon, and it transmits messages in the form of electrochemical waves called nerve impulses.

Q: 4. Skin is also considered as excretory organ, why?

Ans: The excretory system removes non-solid wastes from the body through sweat, urine and exhalation. Sweat leaves the body through the skin and carries waste materials out with it. Therefore, along with the kidneys (urine) and the lungs (exhalation), the skin also works as an excretory organ.

Q: 5. Draw and label the structure of a neuron.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Draw a nerve cell (neuron) as shown in Fig 1.5 of the unit. On the right, draw the large, star-shaped cell body, the thicker region of the neuron, with a round nucleus in its centre and most of the cytoplasm around it. From the cell body, draw many short, thread-like, branching projections in all directions and label them Dendrites. From one side of the cell body, draw one long projection running to the left and label it Axon (the conducting fiber); this is the part that carries impulses away from the cell body. Around the axon, draw a series of bead-like fatty coverings and label them Myelin sheath (insulating fatty layer that speeds transmission), ending in small branches at the far end of the axon. Label the whole drawing: Dendrites, Cell body, Nucleus, Axon (the conducting fiber) and Myelin sheath.

Q: 6. Differentiate between: Receptors and effectors.

Ans: Receptors are the special organs, tissues or cells which detect stimuli, for example the heat and pain receptors present in the skin. Effectors are the parts of the body which produce responses, such as muscles and glands. In short, receptors receive the stimulus and start the nerve impulse, while effectors carry out the response ordered by the central nervous system.

Q: 7. Differentiate between: Voluntary and involuntary actions with examples.

Ans: Voluntary actions are performed under conscious control: you are conscious of what you are doing, and your brain receives nerve impulses from the environment and analyses them for action; for example, you pick up a glass of juice, and you clap hands while watching a cricket match. Involuntary (autonomic) actions are performed unconsciously: you have no consciousness of what your organs are doing, and these actions are regulated by your autonomic nervous system; for example, your heart beats, your intestines digest food, and you blink your eyes.

Q: 8. Differentiate between: Lithotripsy and dialysis.

Ans: Lithotripsy is the method used to remove medium sized kidney stones: it involves bombardment of shock waves on the stones from outside the body, the shock waves break the stones into small pieces, and these pieces are passed out of the body through urine. Dialysis is the cleaning of blood by artificial methods, done by a machine called a dialyzer when the kidneys fail: the patient's blood is passed through the dialyzer and the dialysis fluid flowing around its tubes removes the waste materials, after which the cleaned blood is returned to the body.

Q: 9. Explain the central neurons systems.

Ans: The central nervous system (CNS) acts as the control centre of the whole nervous system. It comprises the brain and the spinal cord. The brain, enclosed in the bony cranium, is divided into fore brain, mid brain and hind brain and controls senses, learning, thinking, memory and body actions, while the spinal cord, an extension of the medulla oblongata located in the vertebral column, connects the brain to the nerves found throughout the body. The CNS processes the messages received through sensory neurons and transmits nerve impulses to motor neurons so that responses are produced.

Q: 10. Explain reflex action with the help of an example and diagram.

Ans: An immediate and involuntary response to a stimulus is called a reflex action; these are sudden, automatic responses shown without the will of the person. Example: when you touch a hot object, the heat is a stimulus which is received by the cells (receptors) of the skin, and a nerve impulse is created in the sensory neuron present in the skin. The sensory neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord, where the inter neuron processes it within no time and transmits it to the motor neuron. The motor neuron carries the impulse to the arm muscles (effectors), the muscles contract and the hand is pulled back. The pathway of nerve impulses which completes a reflex action is called a reflex arc, and it consists of a receptor, a sensory neuron, an inter neuron, a motor neuron and effectors. Diagram (in words): Draw a hand touching a hot pot at the lower left and label the skin of the hand 'Receptors = Heat/Pain, Receptors in skin'. From the hand, draw a line going up to an oval spinal cord cross-section on the right and label the line 'Sensory neuron'. Inside the spinal cord, label the connecting neuron 'Relay neuron', and label the cord itself 'Spinal cord (CNS)', with a small line leaving the top of the cord labelled 'message to brain'. From the spinal cord, draw a second line back down to the arm and label it 'Motor neuron', ending at the arm muscle labelled 'Effector = Muscle in arm'.

Q: 11. Describe the role of kidneys in excretion of waste.

Ans: Blood carrying nitrogenous waste materials from the body is brought to the kidneys by incoming blood vessels called arterioles. Inside the kidneys, the blood containing nitrogenous waste reaches the glomerulus, where most of the excess water and waste materials are filtered from the blood into the Bowman's capsule. The blood, after losing its waste material, goes into the outgoing arteriole and the clean blood is brought back to the main circulatory system. The waste material and excess water pass from the Bowman's capsule into the renal tubule, then through the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle and the distal tubule into the collecting duct in the form of urine. The urine drains into the renal pelvis, passes through the ureter to the urinary bladder, and is finally passed out of the body through the urethra.

Q: 12. A person with kidney disease could be treated either by using a dialysis machine or by a kidney transplant operation. Compare the advantages and disadvantages of these two methods of treatment and how long does a transplanted kidney last.

Ans: Dialysis is the cleaning of blood by artificial methods, done by a machine called a dialyzer: the blood of the patient is passed through the dialyzer, whose dialysis fluid removes the waste materials from the blood, and the cleaned blood is returned to the body. Its advantage, as described in the unit, is that the blood is cleaned without removing or replacing the kidney; its disadvantage is that the kidney itself is not cured, so the cleaning has to be done artificially by the machine again and again. In a kidney transplant, a kidney donated by a healthy person is grafted in the body of the patient to replace the damaged kidney, and the donor may be a blood relative or any other close relative having the same blood group. Its advantage is that the patient gets a working kidney in place of the damaged one; its disadvantage, as described in the unit, is that it needs a suitable donor of the same blood group and an operation to graft the kidney. Note: this unit of the textbook does not state how long a transplanted kidney lasts, so no period can be given from the book.

Project Work

Q: 1. Project: Using recycled materials, make a model showing the structure of kidney and outline the structure and functioning of a kidney tubule.

Ans: Model (in words): Make a bean-shaped model of the kidney, dark brown in colour, with a convex outer surface and a concave inner surface, as the human kidney lies in the abdominal region, one on either side of the vertebral column. Cut the model open to show the three internal regions: the outermost renal cortex, the middle renal medulla and the inner renal pelvis, where urine is drained. Inside it, show a nephron, the structural and functional unit of the kidney (each kidney has over one million nephrons): first the renal corpuscle, made of the glomerulus (a cluster of blood capillaries) enclosed in the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule, then the renal tubule joined to it, in three parts — the first coiled proximal tubule, the U-shaped loop of Henle, and the again coiled distal tubule opening into a collecting duct. Functioning of the kidney tubule: urine is formed in these tubules; the waste material and excess water filtered into the Bowman's capsule pass through the proximal tubule, the loop of Henle and the distal tubule into the collecting duct as urine, and many collecting ducts join and drain the urine out of the nephrons into the renal pelvis.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A gene is a short segment of DNA and the basic physical and functional unit of heredity; genes occur in pairs, one member from the male and the other from the female.
  • DNA stands for Deoxyribonucleic Acid and is made up of nucleotides: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).
  • Chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus, made up of DNA and a protein called Histone; humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes.
  • Meiosis occurs in the germ cells and produces four daughter cells (gametes) with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell.
  • Inheritable characters include eye colour, height, attached and detached earlobes and intelligence; a body organ lost or weakened due to disease is not transferred to offsprings.
  • Eye colour depends on brown pigment in the iris: more pigment gives black eyes, and very less pigment gives light brown eyes.
  • Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, which increases the number of body cells during growth and development.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: DNA

Ans: DNA — Gene. DNA has short segments called genes. These genes are transferred from parents to children and carry the traits of the parents to the offsprings, so a gene is a part of DNA.

Q: 2. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Free earlobe

Ans: Free earlobe — Heritable character. Detached (free) and attached earlobes are inheritable characters, because they are controlled by genes and can pass from one generation to the next generation.

Q: 3. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Mitosis

Ans: Mitosis — Two identical daughter cells. In mitosis a parent cell divides into two daughter cells, the number of chromosomes in the daughter cells remains the same as in the parent cell, and the daughter cells are genetically identical to one another and to the parent cell.

Q: 4. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Chromosome in humans

Ans: Chromosome in humans — 23 pairs. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes in their cells, as stated in the Science TidBit and Key Points of this unit.

Q: 5. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Adenine

Ans: Adenine — Thymine. Adenine (A) and thymine (T) are two of the four types of nucleotides that make up DNA; the other two are guanine (G) and cytosine (C).

Q: 6. Define the following terms: Gene

Ans: A gene is a short segment of DNA. It is the basic physical and functional unit of heredity. Genes are transferred from parents to children and carry the traits of the parents to the offsprings. Genes occur in pairs, and a pair of genes controls each heredity characteristic, e.g. eye colour and height. One member of a gene pair comes from the male and the other from the female.

Q: 7. Define the following terms: DNA

Ans: DNA stands for Deoxyribonucleic Acid. It is the heredity material present in the chromosomes, and it carries all the information from parents to offsprings. DNA is made up of units called nucleotides. The four types of nucleotides are adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T). DNA is coiled many times around proteins, which provides structural support to the chromosome.

Q: 8. Define the following terms: Chromosome

Ans: Chromosomes are thread-like structures present in the nucleus of each cell. They are made up of Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) and a protein called Histone. DNA is coiled many times around these proteins, which provides structural support to the chromosome. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes.

Q: 9. Where does meiosis takes place in the human body? How many cells are produced from parent cell, when it divides by meiosis?

Ans: Meiosis occurs in the germ cells of an organism. In meiosis a parent cell divides into four daughter cells (gametes), in such a way that the number of chromosomes in the daughter cells is half to that of the parent cell. The gametes so produced are genetically different from one another and also from the parent cell, and meiosis involves double cell divisions.

Q: 10. Write any four inheritable characters and three non-inheritable characters.

Ans: Inheritable characters are the characters which can pass from one generation to the next generation. Four examples from the unit are: eye colour, height, attached and detached earlobes, and intelligence. Non-inheritable characters are those which are not transferred to the next generation. Three examples of the kind given in the unit are: a body organ lost due to disease, a body organ weakened due to disease, and any such acquired change in the body during life — the unit explains that if a body organ of a person is lost or weakened due to disease, this character is not transferred to offsprings.

Q: 11. How does the amount of pigment affect the eye colour in human beings?

Ans: The colour of eyes is controlled by a pair of genes, and the genes control the production of brown pigment in the iris of the eyes. If the genes work and produce more pigment, the eyes are black. Production of very less pigment results in light brown eyes. Blue, green and hazel eye colours are developed due to the production of brown pigment in different amounts.

Q: 12. Explain heredity.

Ans: The transfer of characteristics from parents to offsprings is called heredity. Chromosomes, DNA and genes form the basis of heredity. Genes carry the traits or characteristics of the parents to the offsprings. This is the reason that siblings resemble one another and their parents, and plants grown from seeds resemble their parent plant. Eye colour, hair colour, detached or attached ear lobes, intelligence and height are examples of heredity characteristics.

Q: 13. Explain the need for the production of genetically identical cells.

Ans: Genetically identical cells are produced by mitosis, in which a parent cell divides into two daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell, so the daughter cells are genetically similar to one another and to the parent cell. This type of cell division results in the increase of the number of body cells during growth and development. A living organism consists of cells, and a cell has to grow to its full size before it divides, so without the repeated production of identical body cells the organism could not grow and develop.

Q: 14. Write down the differences between mitosis and meiosis with the help of diagrams.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Fig 2.1 Mitosis shows a Parent cell, an arrow down to a cell labelled DNA replicates, then two arrows down to 2 daughter cells. Fig 2.2 Meiosis (printed as 'Metosis' under the figure) shows a Parent cell, an arrow down to a cell labelled DNA replicates, then two arrows down to 2 daughter cells, then arrows down again to 4 daughter cells. Differences: (1) Mitosis occurs in all somatic/body cells of an organism; meiosis occurs in the germ cells of an organism. (2) In mitosis two daughter cells are formed; in meiosis four daughter cells are formed. (3) In mitosis daughter cells have a complete set of chromosomes, identical to the parent cell; in meiosis daughter cells have half the number of chromosomes as compared to the parent cell. (4) In mitosis the daughter cells are genetically identical; in meiosis the daughter cells are genetically different. (5) Mitosis involves a single division; meiosis involves double cell divisions.

Q: 15. Give any four characteristics of humans which are affected by the heredity. Explain any one of them is detail.

Ans: Four characteristics of humans affected by heredity, as given in the unit, are: eye colour, hair colour, detached or attached ear lobes (earlobes), and height (intelligence is also given in the unit). One in detail — eye colour: The colour of eyes in an organism is controlled by a pair of genes. The genes control the production of brown pigment in the iris of the eyes. If the genes work and produce more pigment, the eyes are black. Production of very less pigment results in light brown eyes. Blue, green and hazel eye colours are developed due to the production of brown pigment in different amounts.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Insulin for diabetics is prepared by joining the insulin gene with a plasmid inserted into a bacterium.
  • DNA has a double helical structure, and DNA replication begins with the unwinding of the double helix.
  • Growth hormones are biotechnology products useful for stimulating growth.
  • Genetic modification can be produced by removal, addition or modification of a gene.
  • In DNA replication, each daughter DNA molecule has one new strand and one strand of parent DNA.
  • Biotechnology products used in daily life include yogurt, cheese, bread, vinegar, vaccines and antibiotics.
  • A restriction enzyme is used to cut the gene of interest from the DNA of the donor organism.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Plasmid

Ans: Plasmid — Bacterium. Each bacterium has a single chromosome in the cytoplasm along with an extra chromosomal DNA molecule called plasmid, which is also known as vector. The plasmid can be easily isolated from a bacterial cell and a gene can be attached with it, so the plasmid acts as a carrier of a foreign gene.

Q: 2. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Diabetes

Ans: Diabetes — Insulin. Insulin is a biotechnology product useful for diabetics. It is prepared by joining the insulin gene with a plasmid (vector) inserted into the bacterium.

Q: 3. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Growth hormone

Ans: Growth hormone — Stimulating growth. Growth hormones are biotechnology products used to save lives, and they are useful for stimulating growth, as shown in the table in the Health section of this unit.

Q: 4. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: Double helix

Ans: Double helix — DNA. DNA has a double helical structure. The first step in DNA replication is the unwinding of the double helical structure of the DNA molecule, after which the two strands separate from each other.

Q: 5. Match the words of column A with suitable words of column B: GMOs

Ans: GMOs — modified genes. GMOs are genetically modified organisms. Genetic modification is the change in the genetic organization of an organism using biotechnological techniques, produced by removal, addition or modification of gene, and the organisms whose genes are modified are called genetically modified organisms (GMOs) or transgenic organisms.

Q: 6. Define biotechnology.

Ans: The use of living organisms or their products for the welfare of mankind is called Biotechnology. The ultimate goal of this field is to improve the yield of products from living organisms by making modifications in their DNA.

Q: 7. Write some important products of biotechnology.

Ans: Some important products of biotechnology used in daily life are: bakery products, yogurt, cheese, bread and vinegar; food crops modified by biotechnology; different medicines e.g. insulin for diabetes, vaccines and antibiotics; and biodiesel, washing detergents, sugars and plastics etc. Products used to save lives include insulin (useful for diabetics), vaccines (used against many infectious diseases) and growth hormones (useful for stimulating growth).

Q: 8. What are genetically modified organisms?

Ans: Genetic modification is the change in the genetic organization of an organism using biotechnological techniques. This change can be produced by removal, addition or modification of gene. The organisms whose genes are modified are called genetically modified organisms (GMOs) or transgenic organisms. An organism that contains a foreign gene in its cell is also called a transgenic organism, and the bacterium which takes in the recombinant DNA is called genetically modified bacterium (GM bacterium) or transgenic bacterium.

Q: 9. What is DNA replication? Explain.

Ans: DNA has a unique property to replicate itself. During the replication process, the DNA makes similar copies of itself. DNA replication takes place in the nucleus during cell division. Steps: The first step in DNA replication is the unwinding of the double helical structure of the DNA molecule, and the two strands separate from each other. In the second step, each of these strands produces a new strand using all the four types of nucleotides present in the nucleus. In this way, one DNA molecule produces two daughter DNA molecules. Each DNA molecule has one new strand and one strand of parent DNA, and the two daughter DNA molecules are the exact replicas of each other.

Q: 10. Draw a labeled diagram of bacterium.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Fig 3.3 Bacterium shows a single rod-shaped (oval) bacterial cell drawn diagonally, covered with many short hair-like projections, with a long whip-like tail at the lower end. Every label in the figure is: Capsule (the outermost covering, labelled at the top), Cell wall, Membrane, Cytoplasm (the inside material of the cell, labelled on the left), Pili (the short hair-like projections on the surface, labelled on the right), DNA (the coiled genetic material inside the cell, labelled on the right), Plasmid (the small extra circular DNA inside the cell, labelled on the right below DNA), Ribosome (small structures inside the cell, labelled at the lower right), and Flagellum (the long whip-like tail at the bottom, used for movement).

Q: 11. Explain the process of introducing gene into bacteria.

Ans: Genetic engineering is an advanced technique in biotechnology in which scientists select and isolate the useful gene from one organism and insert it into another organism, usually into a bacterium. The process is: 1. The first step is the identification and isolation of gene (gene of interest) from donor organism. 2. An enzyme called restriction enzyme is used to cut the gene from the DNA of donor organism. 3. The isolated gene is then attached with plasmid DNA taken from a bacterium. The attached gene and plasmid DNA are collectively called recombinant DNA. 4. The recombinant DNA is then introduced into a bacterium, the bacterium starts dividing and produces a bacterial colony. Thus every bacterium of the colony contains the desired gene and hence they produce the desired product (Protein). The organism that contains a foreign gene in its cell is called a transgenic organism.

Q: 12. Describe the role of biotechnology in agriculture and health.

Ans: Agriculture: Biotechnology has played an important role in improving agricultural yield. Herbicides (weed killing chemicals) and pesticides (insect killing chemicals) are used to eliminate weeds and insects and thus protect crops. Using biotechnology, scientists insert weed resistant and pest resistant gene into plants. Cultivation of such genetically modified crops improves the quality of crops and makes them safe for human use. Proteins in foods may be modified to increase their nutritional qualities, and proteins in legumes and cereals may be transformed to provide the amino acids needed by human beings for a balanced diet. Biotechnology also improves the taste, texture and appearance of the food. The major crops that have been modified are maize, wheat, rice, potato, corn and soybean. Health: Biotechnology techniques are also used for curing diseases and improving health. Identification of causes of diseases, production of medicines and correction of genetic defects etc. are the major contributions of biotechnology. One example is the preparation of insulin by joining its gene with a plasmid (vector) inserted into the bacterium. Various biotechnology products that are used to save lives include insulin (useful for diabetics), vaccines (used against many infectious diseases) and growth hormones (useful for stimulating growth).

Q: 13. Describe the role of biotechnology in meeting the nutritional needs of human beings.

Ans: Biotechnology plays a vital role in meeting the nutritional needs of human population. We can enhance food production and nutrition by improvements in livestock and plants using different techniques of biotechnology such as tissue culture and genetic engineering etc. Tissue culture is an important technique of biotechnology, and we can get the types of crops and other plants which give more production using this technique. Similarly, genetic engineering is used in animals for better production of milk and meat. For example, Neeli Ravi buffalo is produced for better production of milk and Nancy sheep for production of more meat. Such animals are very helpful in meeting the nutritional needs. In short, biotechnology has a great importance in human life, and we can succeed in meeting our food problems through biotechnology.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The main air pollutants are carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2), oxides of nitrogen (NO and NO2) and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
  • Greenhouse gases trap a part of the heat reflected back by the earth, which raises the temperature of the atmosphere - the greenhouse effect.
  • CFCs are used in aerosol sprays, as a cooling agent in refrigerators and air conditioners, and in foam packing, and they break down ozone molecules.
  • Effects of deforestation include destruction of habitat for wildlife, soil erosion, less rain, global warming and increasing sea level.
  • Global warming is the rise in the average temperature on earth, and it makes glaciers melt and the level of seawater rise.
  • Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of haemoglobin and damages the central nervous system and heart.
  • Non-renewable resources such as coal, petroleum and natural gas cannot be made available again once depleted, so they must be used carefully.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. What are the main air pollutants?

Ans: The main air pollutants named in the unit are carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2), oxides of nitrogen (NO and NO2) and chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). They are released into the air by human activities and by natural sources, and they harm all living organisms.

Q: 2. Name two greenhouse gases. Why are they called 'greenhouse' gases? Briefly explain.

Ans: Two greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide and methane; the unit also names oxides of nitrogen and water vapours. They are called greenhouse gases because, like the glass panels of a greenhouse, they allow the sun's heat to enter but trap a part of the heat reflected back by the earth. This raises the temperature of the atmosphere, which is known as the greenhouse effect.

Q: 3. How can we conserve our resources?

Ans: Resources can be conserved indirectly through human population control and reducing pollution, and directly through conserving natural resources. Non-renewable resources such as metal ores and fossil fuels (coal, petroleum and natural gas) must be used carefully because they cannot be made available again once depleted. Saving trees, water and electricity, and recycling used paper and other products, also help to conserve resources.

Q: 4. What are the sources of chlorofluorocarbons?

Ans: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are used in aerosol sprays, as a cooling agent in refrigerators and air conditioners, and in foam packing. On leakage from these appliances, CFCs enter the atmosphere and reach the ozone layer, where they break down ozone molecules.

Q: 5. Define deforestation and its effects.

Ans: Deforestation is the cutting and removal of forests for human use, for example for firewood, construction, harvesting land and trade in wood items such as furniture. Its effects listed in the unit are: air pollution, the greenhouse effect, destruction of habitat for wildlife, global warming and increasing sea level, soil erosion, less rain, and sea animals dying.

Q: 6. Which human activities can cause air pollution? What are the negative effects of air pollution?

Ans: Human activities that cause air pollution include the use of vehicles, burning of fuels in factories, industries and thermal power stations, use of aerosol sprays, fertilizers, waste products and insecticides, and deforestation. These activities release pollutants such as carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen into the air. The negative effects are acid rain, which damages vegetation, buildings and aquatic life; eutrophication, the abnormal growth of algae in water bodies; and poisonous ground-level ozone. In the human body, sulphur dioxide causes irritation of eyes, nose and throat, breathing difficulties, pneumonia, asthma, chronic bronchitis, lung cancer, respiratory failure and cardiovascular diseases; oxides of nitrogen damage lung tissues and can cause failure of the heart; and carbon monoxide damages the central nervous system and heart and reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of haemoglobin.

Q: 7. Why it is important to conserve the environment? Give two reasons.

Ans: First, the earth is the only known planet with life on it, and natural resources derived from the environment are essential for our survival, while others satisfy our needs, so they must be protected and preserved. Second, we must conserve resources not only for ourselves but also for future generations: non-renewable resources are formed extremely slowly and cannot be made available once depleted, so careful use today keeps them available for those who come after us.

Q: 8. Define Global warming. What are the causes and effects of global warming?

Ans: Global warming is the rise in the average temperature on earth. It is caused by human activities such as burning of fuels, industries and vehicles, which continually increase the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and speed up the greenhouse effect, so the earth gets warmer and warmer. Its effects are that glaciers melt at an alarming rate, snow on the polar regions and mountains melts faster, causing floods and a rise in the level of seawater, and the climate of many regions of the world changes. Global warming is a serious threat to life on earth, especially to future generations.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In a chemical reaction, new substances are formed that are different from the starting substances, and the atoms are only rearranged.
  • Chemical reactions are of four basic types: addition (synthesis), decomposition, single displacement and double displacement.
  • A balanced chemical equation has the same number of atoms of each element on the reactant side and on the product side.
  • The law of conservation of mass states that matter is neither created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
  • Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings drops; exothermic reactions release heat, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
  • The decompositions of potassium chlorate and calcium carbonate are endothermic and cannot proceed without the addition of heat.
  • When wood burns, the ash left behind weighs less than the wood because gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapours escape into the air.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Note: Two pages of this unit's lesson (printed pages 56-57) are missing from the scanned copy of the book, so that part of the lesson text could not be read. The complete Exercise of this unit is given below; nothing has been guessed or added.

Ans: The missing pages carry lesson text only (the end of one section and the start of 'Changes in states of matter'). Every question of the Unit 5 Exercise is present in the scan and is solved in full.

Q: 2. What are the characteristics of chemical reactions?

Ans: In a chemical reaction new substances are formed which are different from the starting substances; the starting substances are called reactants and the new substances formed are called products. Atoms are rearranged, and matter is neither created nor destroyed, so the total mass of the products is equal to the total mass of the reactants. A chemical change may also be accompanied by a change in the physical state of the substances, for example liquid water is formed from hydrogen gas and oxygen gas. For the chemical equation of a reaction: it must be a true representative of the chemical reaction, the symbols and formulae of reactants and products must be correct, it must be balanced in terms of atoms of reactants and products, and it must show the physical state of the substances involved.

Q: 3. Define chemical reaction and its types.

Ans: The process of formation or breaking of a chemical compound is called a chemical reaction. During a chemical reaction, new substances are formed which are different from the starting substances. Chemical reactions are of four basic types: (i) Addition or synthesis reactions, (ii) Decomposition reactions, (iii) Single displacement or substitution reactions, and (iv) Double displacement reactions.

Q: 4. Explain each type of chemical reaction with one example each.

Ans: i. Addition or synthesis reaction: Two or more substances react together to form one product, A + B -> AB. Example: S + O2 -> SO2 (sulphur + oxygen -> sulphur dioxide). ii. Decomposition reaction: One reactant, which must be a compound, breaks up to form two or more products; these reactions are usually endothermic as they require heat. Example: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (calcium carbonate -> calcium oxide + carbon dioxide). iii. Single displacement reaction: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from its compound. Example: Zn + 2HCl -> H2 + ZnCl2 (zinc displaces hydrogen from hydrochloric acid). iv. Double displacement reaction: Two compounds exchange their ions. Example: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O (hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium chloride + water).

Q: 5. Exothermic reactions are very important in our daily life. Give two reasons.

Ans: Exothermic reactions release heat into the surroundings and are extremely important in daily life. Two reasons from the unit are: (1) The heat released during respiration not only keeps us warm but also provides energy for our normal body functions, and life on earth is possible due to the exothermic reactions taking place in the sun. (2) We enjoy the warmth from the heat released by the combustion of wood, charcoal and natural gas, and the heat released by the burning of fuels is used for cooking food, running vehicles and operating factories.

Q: 6. What is a balanced chemical equation? Why chemical equations need to be balanced?

Ans: A balanced chemical equation is an equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides, i.e. on the side of the reactants and on the side of the products. Chemical equations need to be balanced because, according to the law of conservation of mass, matter is neither created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction. Therefore the number of atoms of each element must be the same before and after the reaction, and coefficients are added to the symbols and formulae until both sides become equal.

Q: 7. Explain the steps for balancing of chemical equations with two examples.

Ans: The simplest method of balancing is the inspection or trial and error method. Step I: Write the unbalanced chemical equation; the symbols and formulae of the reactants and products must be correct. Step II: Count the number of atoms of each element on both sides. Step III: If the numbers of atoms are different on both sides, write the required number as a coefficient of the symbols or formulae. Step IV: Work with one element at a time. Step V: Always start with a relatively small number. Step VI: Start with atoms that appear only once in the reactants and products, and usually leave the diatomic elements like nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen until last. Example 1: CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. Carbon is already balanced (1 on each side). Hydrogen is 4 on the left and 2 on the right, so double the coefficient of H2O: CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. Now oxygen is 2 on the left and 4 on the right, so add coefficient 2 with O2. Balanced equation: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. Example 2: Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2. Balance Fe first by adding coefficient 3 with Fe: 3Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2. Balance oxygen by adding coefficient 4 with H2O: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2. Finally balance hydrogen (8 on the left, 2 on the right) by adding coefficient 4 with H2. Balanced equation: 3Fe + 4H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4H2.

Q: 8. Define Law of conservation of mass. Explain with the help of two examples.

Ans: The law of conservation of mass states that matter is neither created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction. In other words, during a chemical reaction the total mass of the products is equal to the total mass of the reactants, and the number of atoms of each element must be equal on both sides of a chemical equation. Example 1: In the formation of water, 2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l), the atoms of hydrogen and oxygen are only rearranged; no atom is created or destroyed, so the mass of the water formed equals the combined mass of the hydrogen and oxygen used. Example 2: In the balanced equation CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, there are 1 carbon atom, 4 hydrogen atoms and 4 oxygen atoms on both sides, which shows that mass is conserved in the reaction.

Q: 9. When a pile of wood is burnt, the ash left behind is less as compared to wood. How Law of conservation of mass is applicable in this situation?

Ans: When wood burns, it reacts with oxygen of the air and forms ash along with gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapours, which escape into the air. The ash left behind is only the solid product, so its mass appears to be less than the mass of the wood. The law of conservation of mass still applies because the missing mass has not been destroyed; it has gone into the gases released during burning. If the mass of the oxygen used and of all the products, ash plus the escaped gases and vapours, is counted, the total mass of the products is equal to the total mass of the wood and oxygen, so mass is conserved.

Q: 10. Define heat of reaction. Differentiate between exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions, with examples.

Ans: The heat evolved or absorbed during a chemical reaction is called heat of reaction. Heat is either released or absorbed in almost all chemical reactions. Endothermic reactions are those reactions in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings; 'endo' means inside and 'therm' means heat. As a result the temperature of the surroundings drops, and these reactions cannot proceed without the addition of heat. Examples: decomposition of potassium chlorate, 2KClO3 + Heat -> 2KCl + 3O2, and decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3 + Heat -> CaO + CO2. Exothermic reactions are those reactions in which heat is released into the surroundings; 'exo' means outside and 'therm' means heat. As a result the temperature of the surroundings increases. Examples: burning of natural gas (methane), CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + Heat, and formation of ammonia, 3H2 + N2 -> 2NH3 + Heat. Burning is the best example of exothermic reactions.

mcqs.why: A balanced equation has the number of atoms of each element equal on the reactant side and the product side, as required by the law of conservation of mass.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An acid is a substance which provides hydrogen ions H+ in aqueous solution, while an alkali is a water-soluble base which provides hydroxyl ions OH- in aqueous solution.
  • A salt is the chemical compound formed by the neutralization reaction of an acid and a base, for example NaCl from HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O.
  • Acids are sour in taste, turn blue litmus paper to red and turn methyl orange to red.
  • Alkalies are bitter in taste, slippery or soapy to touch, turn red litmus to blue and turn colourless phenolphthalein to pink.
  • A solution with pH below 7 is acidic, a solution with pH 7 is neutral like pure water, and a solution with pH above 7 is alkaline.
  • Bicarbonate toothpaste is alkaline, so it neutralizes the acid produced by plaque on the teeth.
  • Acids react with carbonates to produce salt, water and carbon dioxide gas, for example CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + CO2 + H2O.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Define neutralization reaction and give examples.

Ans: The reaction between an acid and an alkali (base) in which salt and water are formed is called a neutralization reaction. The unit states: acids give salt and water when treated with an alkali, and this reaction is called neutralization reaction; a salt is the chemical compound formed by this reaction. Examples: HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O, and HNO3 + NaOH -> NaNO3 + H2O. Similarly, KOH + HCl -> KCl + H2O.

Q: 2. Why CH3COOH is an acid?

Ans: CH3COOH is acetic acid, the acid present in vinegar, which the unit lists among the uses of acids in food preparations and pickles. It is an acid because, like other acids, it is a substance which provides hydrogen ions H+ in aqueous solution. It also shows the properties of acids: it has a sour taste and it turns blue litmus paper to red.

Q: 3. How will you differentiate between acid, alkali and salt?

Ans: An acid is a substance which provides hydrogen ions H+ in aqueous solution; it is sour in taste, turns blue litmus paper to red and turns methyl orange to red. An alkali is a water-soluble base which provides hydroxyl ions OH- in aqueous solution; it is bitter in taste, is slippery/soapy to touch, turns red litmus to blue and turns colourless phenolphthalein to pink. A salt is a chemical compound formed by the neutralization reaction of an acid and a base, for example NaCl; its aqueous solution conducts electric current, and a salt may be acidic, basic or neutral, so both red and blue litmus stay the same in a neutral salt solution such as NaCl. Indicators and litmus paper are used to identify which of the three a given solution is.

Q: 4. Define acid, alkali and salt. Give two examples of each.

Ans: Acid: A substance which provides hydrogen ions H+ in aqueous solution; the word acid is derived from the Latin word 'acidus' which means sour. Examples: hydrochloric acid HCl and sulphuric acid H2SO4 (also acetic acid in vinegar and citric acid in lemon). Alkali: A substance which provides OH- (hydroxyl) ions in aqueous solution; water-soluble bases are called alkalies. Examples: sodium hydroxide NaOH and potassium hydroxide KOH (also ammonium hydroxide NH4OH). Salt: A chemical compound formed by the reaction of an acid and a base, i.e. by a neutralization reaction. Examples: table salt sodium chloride NaCl and calcium sulphate CaSO4 (also potassium chloride KCl and baking soda NaHCO3).

Q: 5. Plaque is formed on your teeth. Plaque feeds on the sugar left on your teeth if you do not brush your teeth and produces acid. Why is it good to use bicarbonate toothpaste and brush the teeth twice a day?

Ans: Plaque feeds on the sugar left on the teeth and produces acid. This acid attacks and damages the teeth. Bicarbonate toothpaste is alkaline in nature, so it neutralizes the acid produced by plaque in a neutralization reaction and protects the teeth from the acid. Brushing the teeth twice a day removes the plaque and the sugar left on the teeth, so less acid is produced. The unit also notes that magnesium hydroxide, used in toothpaste, is an alkali that neutralises acids.

Q: 6. Describe the physical and chemical properties of acids and alkalies, Give their uses as well.

Ans: Physical properties of acids: they have a sour taste; they turn blue litmus paper to red; they turn methyl orange to red; their aqueous solution conducts electric current; strong acids destroy fabric and cause burns on the skin. Chemical properties of acids: (i) Ionization - acids give hydrogen ion H+ when dissolved in water, e.g. HCl -> H+ + Cl- and H2SO4 -> 2H+ + SO4-2. (ii) Reaction with metals - acids produce salt and hydrogen gas, e.g. Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. (iii) Reaction with alkalis - they give salt and water (neutralization), e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. (iv) Reaction with carbonates - they produce salt, water and carbon dioxide, e.g. CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + CO2 + H2O. Uses of acids: vinegar (acetic acid) is used in pickles and food preparations; citric acid is used in fruit salts and as a food preservative; nitric and sulphuric acids are used in making fertilizers, dyes, paints, drugs and explosives; sulphuric acid is used in car batteries; acids are used to make aqua regia which dissolves gold and platinum. Physical properties of alkalies: they have a bitter taste; they are slippery to touch; they conduct electricity when dissolved in water; strong alkalies damage skin and fabrics; they turn red litmus to blue; they turn colourless phenolphthalein to pink. Chemical properties of alkalies: (i) Ionization - alkalies give hydroxyl ions OH- when dissolved in water, e.g. NaOH -> Na+ + OH- and KOH -> K+ + OH-. (ii) Reaction with acids - they give salt and water, e.g. NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O. (iii) Reaction with fats - alkalies react with fats to produce soap and glycerin: Alkali + Fats -> Soap + Glycerin. Uses of alkalies: ammonia is used for fertilizers and nitric acid; aluminium hydroxide and magnesium hydroxide are used as antacids; calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) is used for whitewash and to neutralize acidity of soil; sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is used in making soaps, detergents and cleaners; magnesium hydroxide is also used in toothpaste.

Q: 7. What is a salt? What are the uses of salt? Give three examples of salts.

Ans: A chemical compound formed by the reaction of an acid and a base is called a salt, and the reaction is called a neutralization reaction, e.g. HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O. Properties of salts: the aqueous solution of a salt conducts electric current, and a salt may be acidic, basic or neutral. Uses of salts from the unit: sodium chloride NaCl is used as table salt, as a preservative and in industries for many sodium compounds; potash alum is used in water purification and as an antiseptic for minor bleeding due to shaving; copper sulphate is used in industry and as a pesticide in agriculture; sodium carbonate is used in making glass and soap, as washing soda, as a household cleaning agent and as a water softener; baking soda NaHCO3 is used as an antacid, in fire extinguishers and in bakeries; magnesium sulphate (Epsom salt) is used as a laxative in medicine to treat constipation. Three examples of salts are: table salt NaCl, calcium sulphate CaSO4 and potassium chloride KCl (baking soda NaHCO3 is another example given in the unit).

Q: 8. Solution (1), Which has a pH of 4 is added to solution (2), Until the mixture has pH of 7. (a) What can you say about solution (1)? (b) What can you say about solution (2)? (c) What can you say about the mixture of 1 and 2?

Ans: (a) Solution (1) has pH 4, which is below 7, so solution (1) is acidic; the pH range of acids is below 7. (b) Solution (2) must be an alkaline solution, with pH above 7, because adding the acidic solution (1) to it brings the pH of the mixture down to 7; the alkali neutralizes the acid. (c) The mixture of 1 and 2 has pH 7, which is the pH of a neutral solution, i.e. like pure water. The acid and the alkali have neutralized each other in a neutralization reaction, forming salt and water, so the final mixture is neutral.

salt and carbon dioxide are formed

provides hydrogen ions H+ in aqueous solution
is bitter in taste and soapy to touch

mcqs.why: The word acid comes from the Latin word 'acidus', which means sour, matching the sour taste of acids.

mcqs.q: Solution (1) has a pH of 4. What can you say about solution (1)?

It is alkaline, because its pH is above 7
It is neutral, like pure water

mcqs.q: Solution (1) of pH 4 is added to solution (2) until the mixture has pH 7. What can you say about solution (2)?
options: It must be an alkaline solution with pH above 7
mcqs.why: Adding the acidic solution (1) brings the pH of solution (2) down to 7, so solution (2) must have been alkaline, with pH above 7; the alkali neutralizes the acid.

options: It is neutral, like pure water, because the acid and alkali have neutralized each other forming salt and water
It still contains only the acid
mcqs.why: pH 7 is the pH of a neutral solution, like pure water. The acid and the alkali have neutralized each other in a neutralization reaction, forming salt and water.

mcqs.q: Bicarbonate toothpaste protects the teeth because:

it is acidic and dissolves plaque
it is alkaline and neutralizes the acid produced by plaque
it forms a salt layer on the teeth
mcqs.why: Plaque produces acid that attacks the teeth; bicarbonate toothpaste is alkaline, so it neutralizes that acid in a neutralization reaction and protects the teeth.

mcqs.q: When an acid reacts with a carbonate, the products are:
mcqs.why: Acids react with carbonates to produce salt, water and carbon dioxide, e.g. CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + CO2 + H2O.

Project Work

Q: 1. Project 1. Apple science! (Group work) Use acids, alkalies and salts from your kitchen for an apple experiment for example vinegar, lemon juice, milk of magnesia, baking soda, etc. Cut the apple in cubes and place in each of these chemicals and find out the colour change of an apple cubes in each of these chemicals and show your working to your teacher and class fellows.

Ans: This is a group practical activity, to be done and shown to the teacher; it has no single written answer. Method from the project as printed: take kitchen acids, alkalies and salts such as vinegar (acetic acid), lemon juice (citric acid), milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide, an alkali) and baking soda (sodium hydrogen carbonate, a salt), cut an apple into cubes, place a cube in each chemical, and observe and record the colour change of the apple cubes in each chemical. The observations are then shown to the teacher and class fellows. The colour changes happen because acids, alkalies and salts react differently with the substances in the apple, in the same way that fruit and flower extracts change colour in acidic and alkaline solutions as described in this unit.

Q: 2. Project 2. Is it true to say that blackboard chalk is calcium carbonate? State a proof for your claim. [Photo caption: Chalk in acid]

Ans: Yes. The proof is the reaction of chalk with an acid, shown in the photo 'Chalk in acid' printed with this project. The unit states that acids and carbonates react to produce salt, water and carbon dioxide gas: for example CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + CO2 + H2O and MgCO3 + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + CO2 + H2O. When chalk is put in acid it fizzes and gives off bubbles of carbon dioxide gas, which is exactly the behaviour of a carbonate. This effervescence on adding acid proves that blackboard chalk is calcium carbonate, CaCO3.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pressure is the perpendicular force exerted on a unit area of a surface; its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), and 1 Pa = 1 N/m2.
  • Pascal's principle: pressure applied on a liquid in a closed container is transferred equally in all directions throughout the liquid.
  • Gas molecules have a very weak force of attraction between them, so a gas can be compressed into less volume.
  • Gas pressure is caused by gas molecules colliding with one another and with the walls of the container.
  • Atmospheric pressure decreases with increase in height from the Earth's surface and is maximum at sea level.
  • At ground level, atmospheric pressure is about 100,000 Pa (100 kPa) and acts in all directions.
  • A hydraulic press is used to compress raw cotton and cloths into bales.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Explain the relationship between force, area and pressure.

Ans: Pressure is the perpendicular force exerted on a unit area of a surface, so Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A). This means pressure increases when the force increases and decreases when the force decreases. For the same force, pressure is greater on a smaller area and smaller on a larger area, so pressure is inversely related to area.

Q: 2. Write a note on Pascal's principle with examples.

Ans: Pascal's principle of fluid-pressure states that pressure applied on a liquid in a closed container is transferred equally in all directions throughout the liquid. It is the working principle of hydraulic systems, in which force is transferred from one place to another with the help of a liquid. Examples given in the unit are the hydraulic press, hydraulic brakes, hydraulic jack and hydraulic lift.

Q: 3. Define pneumatics. How it is related to the force of attraction between gas molecules?

Ans: The study of the behaviour of gases under pressure is called pneumatics. The molecules of a gas are free to move because the force of attraction between them is very weak. Because the molecules are not very close together, a gas can be squeezed into less space or volume; this is called compressing a gas, and it puts the gas under pressure.

Q: 4. What are aerosols? Write down the applications of gas pressure.

Ans: An aerosol is a suspension of tiny liquid particles in a gas enclosed under pressure, released as a fine spray by means of a propellant gas; an aerosol spray is a can bottle containing a liquid, sealed and fitted with a hollow tube, and when the knob is pressed the liquid is sprayed out in the form of aerosol. Applications of gas pressure given in the unit are: (1) air motion is caused due to difference in air pressure; (2) wheels remain inflated because of gas pressure and traffic keeps flowing on the road; (3) insecticides and pesticides are sprayed through a spray machine because of gas pressure; (4) a syringe is filled due to gas pressure.

Q: 5. Relate the height from the Earth's surface with the atmospheric pressure.

Ans: Atmospheric pressure decreases with increase in height from the Earth's surface. At sea level the mean density of the air is maximum and the atmospheric pressure is maximum. As we go up from sea level, the density of the air decreases, so the pressure also decreases. That is why air pressure at Peshawar is greater than in Murree, which is at a higher altitude.

Q: 6. What is pressure? State its SI unit.

Ans: Pressure is the perpendicular force exerted on a unit area of a surface, i.e. Pressure = Force / Area. Its SI unit is the pascal, denoted by Pa. The unit of force is newton (N) and that of area is square meter (m2), so 1 pascal = 1 N/m2.

Q: 7. What are the causes of gas pressure?

Ans: When a container is filled with a gas, the gas molecules collide with one another as well as with the walls of the container, and thus they exert pressure on the walls of the container. Experiments show that the pressure of a gas depends on its quantity and also on its temperature: (1) if the temperature rises, the motion of the molecules and the pressure increase due to more collisions of molecules with the walls of the container; (2) on increasing the quantity of the gas in the container, the number of collisions of molecules also increases, thus increasing the pressure in the container, as when a bicycle tyre tube bursts if it is filled with more air.

Q: 8. What is a hydraulic press? Write its application.

Ans: A hydraulic press is a machine which works on Pascal's principle. It consists of two cylinders, one of large cross-sectional area and the other of small cross-sectional area, connected with a tube, with pistons fitted at the openings of both cylinders, which are filled with fluid (water, oil etc.). When the small piston is moved down with a force, it exerts pressure which is transmitted through the fluid to the larger piston; the large piston moves up and compresses the thing placed over it. Its application given in the unit is that the hydraulic press is used to compress raw cotton, cloths etc. into bales.

Q: 9. Define atmospheric pressure and how it's value changes with the height from the sea level.

Ans: The atmosphere, because of its weight, exerts a pressure on the surface of the earth, which is called atmospheric pressure. It acts in all directions, and around us at ground level it is about 100,000 Pa or 100 kPa. At sea level, the mean density of the air is maximum and the atmospheric pressure is maximum. As we go up from sea level, the density of the air decreases, so atmospheric pressure decreases with increase in height from the Earth's surface.

mcqs.q: For the same force, what happens to the pressure when the area becomes smaller?
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area, so pressure is inversely related to area: for the same force, pressure is greater on a smaller area and smaller on a larger area.

mcqs.q: According to Pascal's principle, pressure applied on a liquid in a closed container is:
options: transferred equally in all directions throughout the liquid
mcqs.why: Pascal's principle of fluid-pressure states that pressure applied on a liquid in a closed container is transferred equally in all directions throughout the liquid; hydraulic systems work on this principle.

mcqs.q: A gas can be squeezed into less space (compressed) because:
options: its molecules are very close together
its molecules are strongly attracted to each other
the force of attraction between its molecules is very weak
mcqs.why: The molecules of a gas are free to move because the force of attraction between them is very weak, and because they are not very close together, a gas can be squeezed into less space or volume.

mcqs.q: What is an aerosol?
options: A liquid stored without any gas
A solid powder kept in a can
A suspension of tiny liquid particles in a gas enclosed under pressure
mcqs.why: An aerosol is a suspension of tiny liquid particles in a gas enclosed under pressure, released as a fine spray by means of a propellant gas when the knob of the can is pressed.

mcqs.q: How does atmospheric pressure change as height from the Earth's surface increases?
mcqs.why: Atmospheric pressure decreases with increase in height from the Earth's surface, because the density of the air decreases as we go up; at sea level the density and the pressure are maximum.

mcqs.q: Atmospheric pressure at ground level is about 100,000 Pa. What force does it exert on an area of 1 m2?
mcqs.why: Step 1: Pressure = Force / Area, so Force = Pressure x Area. Step 2: Force = 100,000 Pa x 1 m2. Step 3: Since 1 Pa = 1 N/m2, Force = 100,000 x 1 = 100,000 N.

mcqs.q: What happens to the pressure of a gas in a container when its temperature rises?
options: The pressure increases due to more collisions of molecules with the walls
mcqs.why: When the temperature rises, the motion of the gas molecules increases and they collide more with the walls of the container, so the pressure exerted on the walls increases.

mcqs.q: A hydraulic press consists of:
options: two pistons of equal size only
a cylinder filled with gas only
two cylinders of large and small cross-sectional area connected by a tube, with pistons and filled with fluid
mcqs.why: A hydraulic press consists of two cylinders, one of large and the other of small cross-sectional area, connected with a tube, with pistons fitted at both openings and filled with fluid such as water or oil.

mcqs.q: Around us at ground level, atmospheric pressure is about:
mcqs.why: The atmosphere, because of its weight, exerts atmospheric pressure; it acts in all directions and around us at ground level it is about 100,000 Pa or 100 kPa.

mcqs.q: 1 pascal (Pa) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Pressure = Force / Area; the unit of force is the newton (N) and the unit of area is the square meter (m2), so 1 pascal = 1 N/m2.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The seven base quantities are length (metre), mass (kilogram), time (second), temperature (kelvin), electric current (ampere), intensity of light (candela) and amount of substance (mole).
  • Physical quantities are divided into two categories: base quantities and derived quantities.
  • SI units are used throughout the world, so scientists everywhere use the same agreed set of units.
  • 1000 cm = 10 meters and 10,000 millimeters.
  • For a correct volume reading, keep the eye on a level with the bottom of the meniscus; mercury's meniscus curves upward, unlike other liquids.
  • Prefixes: kilo means 1000, centi means 1/100, and milli means 1/1000.
  • 1 cubic meter = 1000 litre, 1 litre = 1000 milli-litre, and 1 second is 1/86400 part of a mean solar day.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Write seven base physical quantities along with their SI units.

Ans: The seven base physical quantities and their SI units given in the unit are: Length - Meter (m); Mass - Kilogram (kg); Time - Second (s); Temperature - Kelvin (K); Electric current - Ampere (A); Intensity of light - Candela (cd); Amount of substance - Mole (mol). Base quantities are those in terms of which other physical quantities can be defined.

Q: 2. Write the uses of units in our daily life.

Ans: In daily life we use SI units for measurement: the metre is used as a unit for the measurement of length; the kilogram is used as a unit for the measurement of mass of different things; the cubic meter (m3) is the SI unit for the measurement of volume, while in daily life the volume of liquids is measured in litres; and the second (s) is the unit of time. Measurements are part of our daily life and play an important role in describing and understanding the physical world.

Q: 3. Why scientists prefer SI units?

Ans: In the past, the system of units of one country was different from that of another country. The System International (SI) units are now used throughout the world and are convenient for daily use. Scientists particularly prefer this system for the exchange of their scientific researches and informations with the world's scientific community, because everyone uses the same agreed set of units.

Q: 4. Convert 1000 centimeters into meters and millimeters.

Ans: Given: Length = 1000 centimeters (cm) Formula: 1 centimetre = 1/100 metre, so metres = centimetres / 100; and 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres, so millimetres = centimetres x 10 Substitution: Metres = 1000 / 100 = 10 m; Millimetres = 1000 x 10 = 10,000 mm Answer: 1000 cm = 10 meters and 10,000 millimeters

Q: 5. Physical quantities are divided in how many categories?

Ans: Physical quantities are divided into two categories: base quantities and derived quantities. Base quantities are those in terms of which other physical quantities can be defined, e.g. mass, length and time. The physical quantities that are expressed in terms of base quantities are called derived quantities, e.g. volume, speed, density and area.

Q: 6. What are international system units? How they are used in daily life?

Ans: In the middle of the last century, an international committee agreed on a set of units to measure physical quantities; this set of units is called System International units, denoted by SI. This system is now used throughout the world and its units are convenient for daily use. In daily life, the metre is used to measure length, the kilogram to measure mass of different things, the cubic meter (m3) and the litre to measure volume (1 cubic meter = 1000 litre; 1 litre = 1000 milli-litre), and the second to measure time, where 1 second is 1/86400 part of a mean solar day.

Q: 7. What is meniscus?

Ans: When a liquid is poured into a measuring cylinder, the surface of the liquid curves upwards at the point where it touches the inside of the cylinder. This curvature is called the meniscus. The volume is noted on the scale in front of the meniscus of the liquid. The meniscus of all liquids is curved downward except for mercury, which has a meniscus curved upward when put in a cylindrical container.

Q: 8. Give in detail the procedure of measuring the volume of a liquid by reading correct meniscus in the measuring cylinder.

Ans: A measuring cylinder is used to measure the volume of a liquid; it is made up of transparent plastic or glass and has a vertical scale in millilitres (ml) or cubic centimetres (cm3). Pour the liquid into the cylinder and read the volume from the scale on the side. For correct measurement of the volume, the cylinder must be placed on a horizontal surface and the eye should be kept on a level with the bottom of the meniscus, and the volume is noted on the scale in front of the meniscus of the liquid. Reading from above or below the level gives a wrong volume, as shown in Fig 8.6 (19.82 ml and 19.62 ml are wrong readings; 19.70 ml at eye level is correct).

Q: 9. What are prefixes? Explain their role in System international units.

Ans: Prefixes are the words or letters added before SI units, such as milli, centi and kilo. The values of these prefixes are multiples and sub-multiples of 10: kilo (k) means 1000 (thousand), centi (c) means 1/100 (one hundredth part) and milli means 1/1000 (one thousandth part). Prefixes are useful to express very large or small quantities, and they are used for the inter conversion of smaller units and bigger units: when the prefix kilo is added before a unit, its value is increased by 1000, e.g. 1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metre (m) and 1 kilogram (kg) = 1000 gram; when centi is added, the value is decreased by 1/100 part, e.g. 1 centimetre = 1/100 metre; and when milli is added, the value is decreased by 1/1000 part, e.g. 1 millimetre = 1/1000 metre and 1 milligram = 1/1000 gram.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of temperature?
mcqs.why: Temperature is one of the seven base physical quantities, and the SI unit given for it in the unit is the kelvin (K).

mcqs.q: Why do scientists prefer SI units?
options: Because each country has its own SI units
Because everyone uses the same agreed set of units for exchanging research
Because SI units cannot be converted
Because SI units are used in only one country
mcqs.why: In the past, the system of units of one country was different from that of another. SI units are now used throughout the world, so scientists can exchange their scientific researches and informations using the same agreed set of units.

mcqs.q: 1000 centimeters is equal to how many meters?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1 centimetre = 1/100 metre, so metres = centimetres / 100. Step 2: 1000 / 100 = 10. So 1000 cm = 10 meters.

mcqs.q: 1000 centimeters is equal to how many millimeters?
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres, so millimetres = centimetres x 10. Step 2: 1000 x 10 = 10,000. So 1000 cm = 10,000 millimeters.

mcqs.why: Physical quantities that are expressed in terms of base quantities are called derived quantities; the unit lists volume, speed, density and area as derived quantities, while mass, length and time are base quantities.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Heat is a form of energy transferred due to a difference in temperature; its SI unit is the joule, and a calorie raises 1 gram of water by 1 Celsius degree.
  • The density of water is maximum at 4°C: water contracts on heating from 0°C to 4°C and expands on heating from 4°C to 100°C.
  • A fire alarm uses a bimetallic strip of brass and iron; on heating it bends, touches a screw, completes the circuit and the bell rings.
  • Mercury is preferred over alcohol in a clinical thermometer because its boiling point is very high and its expansion is uniform; normal human body temperature is 36.9°C or 98.4°F.
  • Telephone and electrical wires are given sag so they can contract in winter without breaking.
  • Railway tracks are laid in sections with gaps, joined by fish plates, so the rails have room to expand in hot weather.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Define heat? What units are used for its measurement?

Ans: Heat is a form of energy. It is transferred from one body to another due to difference in temperature. The SI unit for measuring heat is the joule: 1 Joule = 1 newton.meter = 1 kg.m2/s2. The calorie is also used; a calorie is the heat required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of water by 1 Celsius degree.

Q: 2. Explain the peculiar behavior of water?

Ans: Liquids in general expand on heating and contract on cooling, but the expansion of water is a little different. When water is heated from 0°C to 4°C it contracts instead of expanding, and when it is further heated from 4°C up to its boiling point (100°C) it expands just like other liquids. In the same way, when water is cooled down from 100°C to 4°C it contracts, but when it is further cooled from 4°C to 0°C it expands and its volume increases. This increase in volume on cooling from 4°C to 0°C is known as the anomalous expansion or peculiar behavior of water. It means that the density of water is maximum at 4°C. Under frozen water during winters, aquatic life is able to survive in the water below the ice because ice acts as an insulator.

Q: 3. Which component expands on heating in fire alarms and how it works?

Ans: The component is the bimetallic strip of brass and iron, used in the circuit of the electric fire alarm (Fig 9.5, with labels Clamp, Bimetallic strip, Brass, Iron, Screw / Contact and Battery). When a fire occurs, the heat of the fire causes the brass and iron strips to expand differently, causing the bimetallic strip to bend. On bending, the strip touches the screw adjacent to it, thus completing the circuit. Once the circuit is completed, the bell begins to ring.

Q: 4. Describe the sources and effects of heat.

Ans: Sources of heat: (1) The Sun is the main source of heat. (2) In our daily life, we get heat from the burning of wood and fossil fuels i.e. oil, gas and coal. (3) Heat may be produced by friction: whenever two bodies are rubbed against each other, heat is produced, as by rubbing flintstones in ancient times, or rubbing our hands together until they feel warm. (4) Electricity is also a source of heat: whenever electricity is passed through a metal wire, it gets hot. (5) Heat is also produced by certain chemical reactions, e.g. the biochemical reactions in our body produce heat, and when CaO is added in water, heat is produced. Effects of heat: heat can cause (i) changes in the state of matter, (ii) chemical changes, (iii) expansion in solids, liquids and gases, (iv) an increase in temperature, and (v) wind, rain and waves in seas are formed due to increase in temperature.

Q: 5. How Fahrenheit scale is different from Centigrade or Celsius scale.

Ans: In the Centigrade or Celsius scale, the lower standard point or freezing point of ice is marked as 0°C and the upper standard point or boiling point of water is marked as 100°C at normal atmospheric pressure; the distance between these two fixed points is divided into 100 equal parts and each part or division is called a degree centigrade, denoted by °C. In the Fahrenheit scale, the lower standard point or freezing point of ice is marked as 32°F and the upper standard point or boiling point of water is marked as 212°F at normal atmospheric pressure; the distance between these two fixed points is divided into 180 equal parts and each part or division is called a degree Fahrenheit, denoted by °F.

Q: 6. Explain thermal expansion of solids with the help of an activity.

Ans: On heating, the movement of the molecules of a solid increases and the distances between the molecules become larger, which causes thermal expansion; on cooling, the movement becomes slow, the distances become small and the solid contracts. The expansion in length due to heating is called linear expansion, while that in volume is called volumetric expansion. Activity 9.1 (linear expansion): Take a metallic rod about 1 meter in length. Clamp its one end and let its other end rest on a needle. A long needle or a thick wire passes through the end of the straw which acts as a pointer. The labelled apparatus in the figure shows the Knitting needle (rod) resting on two Wooden blocks, Candles on a Tray containing stand below it, and at the free end a Needle, Mirror and Paper scale marked 0 to 5. When the rod is heated by a candle, the pointer moves: the length of the rod has increased, due to which the needle rolls forward and the movement of the pointer can be seen on the paper scale. This activity illustrates linear expansion in a metallic rod. Activity 9.2 similarly shows volumetric expansion: a metallic sphere which passes easily through a ring does not pass after heating, because its diameter and volume have increased, and on cooling it contracts and passes again.

Q: 7. Describe the uses of expansion and contraction of liquids in our daily lives.

Ans: The liquids expand more as compared to solids, and contract on cooling. Due to this property, mercury and alcohol are used in thermometers, the instruments used for measuring temperature. In a common (clinical) thermometer, a glass bulb connected to a thin capillary tube is filled with mercury, which expands into the capillary tube when heated and rises up in the tube to show the temperature; the capillary tube has a constriction just above the bulb which prevents the mercury from falling back during expansion. Mercury is preferred over alcohol because the boiling point of mercury is very high and its expansion is also uniform. When the thermometer is placed under the tongue or in the armpit, the mercury expands due to the heat of the human body and shows the body temperature; the normal human body temperature is 36.9°C or 98.4°F.

Q: 8. Give reasons: Why a sag is given in the telephone or electrical wires?

Ans: The telephone wires between two poles hang down in summer and become tight in winter, because the wires expand on heating and contract on cooling. Overhead telephone or electrical wires between two poles are therefore given a certain amount of sag so that they can contract in winter without breaking. If there is no sag, the wires can break on contraction in winter.

Q: 9. Give reasons: Why mercury is preferred over alcohol in clinical thermometer?

Ans: Mercury and alcohol are both used in thermometers because liquids expand on heating. However, the boiling point of mercury is very high and its expansion is also uniform, and that is why mercury is preferred over alcohol in a clinical thermometer: it can measure higher temperatures without boiling and it rises evenly in the capillary tube, giving a correct reading.

Q: 10. Give reasons: Why railway tracks are laid in sections with gaps between them?

Ans: Railway tracks are subjected to changes in temperature, and solids expand on heating. The railway tracks are therefore laid in sections with gaps between them, and the sections are joined by fish plates, so that the rails have room to expand in hot weather. If there are no gaps in rail tracks, then thermal expansion will cause them to bend, which can damage the track.

It does not expand on heating
Its boiling point is very high and its expansion is uniform
mcqs.why: Mercury is preferred over alcohol because the boiling point of mercury is very high and its expansion is also uniform, so it can measure higher temperatures and rises evenly.

mcqs.q: Why is a sag given in telephone or electrical wires between two poles?
options: So the wires can expand in summer without breaking
So the wires can contract in winter without breaking
So birds can sit on the wires
So the wires stay tight in winter
mcqs.why: Wires expand on heating and contract on cooling; they are given sag so that they can contract in winter without breaking, otherwise contraction could break them.

mcqs.q: Why are railway tracks laid in sections with gaps between them?
options: To let water drain from the track
To join the sections with mercury
To give the rails room to expand in hot weather
To make the rails contract in summer
mcqs.why: Solids expand on heating, so railway tracks are laid in sections with gaps, joined by fish plates, giving room to expand in hot weather; without gaps the rails would bend.

mcqs.q: The normal human body temperature is 36.9°C. What is this in Fahrenheit?
mcqs.why: Full working: °F = °C x 9/5 + 32 = 36.9 x 9/5 + 32 = 66.42 + 32 = 98.42, which is 98.4°F, the value stated for normal human body temperature in the chapter.
