Project Work

Q: 1. Project (a). Draw the diagrams of celsius / centigrade scale and fahrenheit scale thermometers on chart paper and explain their differences with the help of diagrams.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Two thermometer diagrams stand side by side, as in the printed figure captioned 'Celsius and Fahrenheit scale'. The left thermometer is labelled °C at the top; its scale is marked 50, 40, 30, 20, 10, 0, -10, -20, -30 from top to bottom, the red column rises to the 20 mark, and the round bulb at the bottom shows 20°. The right thermometer is labelled °F at the top; its scale is marked 120, 100, 80, 60, 40, 20, 0, -20, -40, the blue column rises to about the 70 mark, and the bulb at the bottom shows 80°. Differences: on the Celsius / centigrade scale the freezing point of ice is 0°C and the boiling point of water is 100°C, and the distance between the two fixed points is divided into 100 equal parts, each one degree centigrade (°C). On the Fahrenheit scale the freezing point of ice is 32°F and the boiling point of water is 212°F, and the distance between the two fixed points is divided into 180 equal parts, each one degree Fahrenheit (°F).

Q: 2. Project (b). Make a chart and describe the features of an ideal energy saving home. Explain why each feature like: use of solar panels on the roof, large double glazed windows, light colour wall paint etc, would be useful.

Ans: An ideal energy saving home uses heat carefully so that less fuel and electricity are wasted. (1) Solar panels on the roof: the Sun is the main source of heat and light, so panels on the roof receive sunlight all day and use the sun's energy for the home, reducing the need to burn fossil fuels (oil, gas and coal) or use electricity for heating and lighting. (2) Large double glazed windows: two sheets of glass with air trapped between them let sunlight and light enter the rooms, while the trapped air acts as an insulator, so heat does not easily escape in winter and outside heat does not easily enter in summer; less energy is then needed to heat or cool the home. (3) Light colour wall paint: light colours reflect the sun's radiant heat instead of absorbing it, so the walls and rooms stay cooler in hot weather and less energy is needed for cooling. Together these features reduce the expansion-and-heating load on the house and save energy.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A ray through the optical centre of a lens goes unrefracted; a ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the principal focus, and a ray through the principal focus becomes parallel after refraction.
  • When the lens of an eye becomes thicker, its focal length is reduced; in short sightedness parallel rays are focused in front of the retina instead of on it.
  • For a convex lens, an object between F and the optical centre forms a virtual, magnified and erect image on the same side as the object.
  • The iris controls the pupil size: the pupil grows larger in the dark and contracts in bright light.
  • The retina acts like a screen on which an inverted image is formed, and the optic nerve carries the image to the brain, which gives an erect view.
  • Long sightedness is corrected by a convex lens of suitable focal length, while short sightedness is corrected by a concave lens.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Describe the paths of the three rays passing through convex lens with the help of ray diagrams.

Ans: Diagram (in words): In each ray diagram a vertical biconvex (convex) lens stands at the centre, its optical centre is marked O, and a horizontal principal axis passes through the lens with F and 2F (or C) marked on both sides. Three particular rays are used, and the image is formed at the position where all three rays, or any two of them, meet. Ray 1 (Fig 10.5 First ray): a ray parallel to the principal axis, after refraction from the convex lens, passes through its principal focus F on the other side. Ray 2 (Fig 10.6 Second ray): a ray passing through the principal focus F of a convex lens, after refraction, becomes parallel to the principal axis. Ray 3 (Fig 10.7 Third ray): a ray passing through the optical centre O of the lens goes unrefracted, continuing straight in the same direction. In a ray diagram, rays of light are represented by straight lines with an arrow head over the line to indicate the direction.

Q: 2. How the focal length is affected when the lens of an eye becomes thicker?

Ans: When the lens of an eye becomes thicker, its focal length is reduced (it becomes shorter). The unit states this for short sightedness: the lens of such an eye becomes thick and the focal length is reduced, and due to this reason parallel rays are focused in front of the retina instead of on it. The opposite also holds in focusing: the eye lens makes small focusing by becoming thinner or thicker, a thicker lens converging the rays more strongly.

Q: 3. Draw ray diagrams to show how a converging lens forms images. What are the characteristics of these images?

Ans: Diagram (in words): A vertical convex (converging) lens stands at optical centre O on a horizontal principal axis, with F and 2F marked on both sides. The upright object is an arrow AB standing on the axis (A at the top, B on the axis); from A one ray goes parallel to the axis and refracts through F on the other side, and one ray goes straight through O unrefracted; the inverted image A'B' (B' on the axis, A' below it) forms where the two rays meet. (a) Object beyond 2F: image A'B' is formed on the other side between F and 2F — real, inverted and smaller in size (Fig 10.8). (b) Object at 2F: image is also formed at 2F on the other side — real, inverted and of the same size (Fig 10.9). (c) Object between 2F and F: image is formed beyond 2F on the other side — real, inverted and large in size (Fig 10.10). (d) Object at F: the rays become parallel after refraction, so the image is formed at infinity on the other side — real, inverted and very large in size (Fig 10.11). (e) Object between F and O: the rays diverge after refraction and do not actually meet on the other side; extended back, they meet on the same side as the object, so a virtual image is formed there — magnified and erect (Fig 10.12, image A'B' shown with dashed lines on the object's side).

Q: 4. Define the following terms related to a lens along with the diagram. (i) Principle axis (ii) Optical centre (iii) Principal focus (iv) Focal length.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Fig 10.4 Convex lens shows a vertical purple biconvex lens labelled 'Imaging lens' at the centre of two large dashed circles (the spheres of which its curved surfaces are parts). A horizontal dashed line labelled 'Principal axis' runs from X on the left to Y on the right, passing through the point labelled 'Center of curvature' C on the left, the 'optical centre' at the middle of the lens, and the 'Focal point' F on the right. Four parallel red rays travel from the left, refract through the lens and converge at the focal point F. A double-headed arrow marked 'f' below the axis, labelled 'focal length', measures the distance from the lens / optical centre to F. Definitions: (i) Principal axis: a line passing through centre of curvature, optical centre and focal point is called principal axis or optical axis. (ii) Optical centre: the mid or central point of a lens is called its optical centre, denoted by 'O'. (iii) Principal focus / Focal point: the point where light rays meet after refraction through the lens, denoted by 'F'. (iv) Focal length: the distance between optical centre 'O' and principal focus 'F' is called focal length, denoted by 'f'.

Q: 5. Write only two uses of concave lens and convex lens.

Ans: Convex lens (any two): (1) In a camera, where the convex lens forms a real, small and inverted image of an object on the film. (2) In spectacles to correct long sightedness, and in optical instruments such as microscopes and telescopes. Concave lens (any two): (1) In spectacles to correct short sightedness, so that the rays are focused on the retina. (2) As biconcave lenses in science laboratories and experiments, and in instruments such as binoculars named in the unit's uses.

Q: 6. Describe the features of a human eye that allows it to see.

Ans: The human eye works like a camera. It consists of an enclosure having a convex lens at one end and a light sensitive surface, the retina, at the other end (Fig 10.16 Structure of a Human Eye labels: Lens, Pupil, Cornea, Iris, Vitreous, Retina, Macula and Optic Nerve). The convex lens system of the eye forms a small inverted image of anything in front of it on the retina. The iris diaphragm has a pupil in the middle of the eye which controls the amount of light going into the eye; the iris controls the pupil size — the pupil grows larger to see things in the dark, whereas it contracts in bright light. The cornea and the watery fluid (vitreous) behind it do most of the focusing of the rays of light, and the lens itself makes small focusing by becoming thinner or thicker; unlike the camera, the eye lens does not move back and forth. The retina acts like a screen on which the inverted image is formed. The optic nerve carries the image from the retina to the brain, which interprets the image, and the brain gives an erect view of the object.

Q: 7. Discuss how the eye and camera are very similar and point out some differences between them.

Ans: Similarities: A camera is basically a box with a convex lens at one end and a light sensitive film placed at the opposite end, just as the eye is an enclosure with a convex lens at one end and the light sensitive retina at the other. In both, the lens forms a real, small and inverted image of an object — on the film in the camera and on the retina in the eye (Fig 10.14 Comparison of camera and human eye). In both, the amount of light entering is controlled: the camera has an adjustable diaphragm which controls the aperture (hole) and the intensity of light entering, and the eye has the iris which controls the pupil size. Differences: (1) Focusing — a distant image on the film is focused by moving the camera lens forward or backward in its holder, whereas the eye lens does not move back and forth; the eye lens focuses by becoming thinner or thicker. (2) The camera's shutter opens and shuts quickly to let light enter for a very short interval, and the amount of light reaching the film depends upon the exposure time and the area of the aperture; the eye instead adjusts its pupil, which expands in darkness and contracts in bright light. (3) The exposed film is processed in chemical solutions in a dark room and printed out, whereas the retina's image is carried by the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets it and gives an erect view.

Q: 8. Write a note on short sightedness and long sightedness and also explain how to remove these defects using lenses?

Ans: Short sightedness: A person suffering from short sightedness cannot see far off objects clearly but can see the nearby objects clearly. The lens of such an eye becomes thick and the focal length is reduced, so parallel rays are focused in front of the retina (Fig 10.17, top diagram: three parallel rays entering the eye meet at a point inside the eye, before the retina). Correction: short sightedness can be corrected by wearing spectacles having concave lenses of suitable focal length, which diverge the rays before they enter the eye (Fig 10.17, bottom diagram: a concave lens in front of the eye spreads the parallel rays, and the eye then focuses them on the retina). As a result, rays are focused on the retina. Long sightedness: A person suffering from long sightedness cannot see near objects clearly but far off objects can be seen clearly. The eye ball becomes thinner or less converging, so parallel rays are focused behind the retina (Fig 10.18, top diagram: the rays meet at a point behind the eyeball). Correction: this defect can be removed by wearing spectacles having a convex lens of suitable focal length (Fig 10.18, bottom diagram: a convex lens in front of the eye converges the rays more, so they focus on the retina), which makes the rays focused at the retina.

Q: 9. Test Yourself Activity i. The diagram shows light rays entering two lenses. What type of lens is (a) lens A? (b) lens B?

Ans: In the printed diagram, three parallel horizontal rays with arrow heads enter each lens from the left. (a) Lens A (top) is drawn thick in the middle and thin at the edges, pointed at both ends: it is a convex (biconvex) lens, also called a converging lens. (b) Lens B (bottom) is drawn thin in the middle and thick at the top and bottom edges, curved inwards on both sides: it is a concave (biconcave) lens, also called a diverging lens.

Q: 10. Test Yourself Activity ii. Copy and complete the diagrams showing the light rays entering and leaving each lens.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Three parallel horizontal rays enter each lens from the left, travelling along and parallel to the principal axis. Lens A (convex / converging lens, thick in the middle): on leaving the lens, the top ray bends downwards, the bottom ray bends upwards and the middle ray continues along the axis; all three rays converge and meet at one point, the focal point F, on the principal axis on the right-hand side of the lens, and after crossing at F they continue onwards, spreading apart. Lens B (concave / diverging lens, thin in the middle): on leaving the lens, the rays diverge — the top ray bends upwards away from the axis and the bottom ray bends downwards away from the axis, while the central ray goes straight; the diverging rays never meet on the right, but if they are traced (extended) back to the left they appear to come from a single point, the (virtual) focal point F, on the same side of the lens as the incoming light.

Q: 11. Test Yourself Activity ii(a). Use diagram A to explain what a focal point is?

Ans: In diagram A, the parallel light rays entering the convex lens are refracted by the lens and all meet (converge) at one point on the principal axis on the other side of the lens. That point, where light rays meet after refraction through the lens, is the focal point (principal focus) of the lens, denoted by 'F'. The distance between the optical centre of the lens and this focal point is the focal length.

Q: 12. Test Yourself Activity ii(b). Name one optical instrument that uses lens A and B

Ans: Lens A is a convex lens: it is used in a camera, whose convex lens forms a real, small and inverted image on the film (convex lenses are also used in microscopes and telescopes). Lens B is a concave lens: concave lenses are used in the spectacles worn to correct short sightedness (biconcave lenses are also used in science laboratories and in binoculars named in the unit).

options: It passes through the principal focus
It becomes parallel to the principal axis
mcqs.why: A ray passing through the optical centre O of the lens goes unrefracted, continuing straight in the same direction, as stated for the third ray.

mcqs.q: A ray passing through the principal focus F of a convex lens, after refraction, becomes:
options: focused in front of the lens
mcqs.why: A ray passing through the principal focus F of a convex lens, after refraction, becomes parallel to the principal axis, as stated for the second ray.

mcqs.q: How is the focal length affected when the lens of an eye becomes thicker?
mcqs.why: When the lens of an eye becomes thicker, its focal length is reduced and becomes shorter, so it converges the rays more strongly.

mcqs.q: For a convex lens, when the object is beyond 2F, the image formed is:
options: virtual, erect and magnified, on the same side
real, inverted and smaller, between F and 2F
real, inverted and of the same size, at 2F
mcqs.why: With the object beyond 2F, the image is formed on the other side between F and 2F and is real, inverted and smaller in size.

options: virtual, magnified and erect, on the same side as the object
mcqs.why: When the object is between F and O, the rays diverge after refraction and meet only when extended back on the object's side, forming a virtual image that is magnified and erect.

mcqs.q: In the Test Yourself diagrams, lens B is thin in the middle and thick at the edges. What type of lens is lens B?
mcqs.why: Lens B, thin in the middle and thick at the top and bottom edges and curved inwards on both sides, is a concave (biconcave) lens, also called a diverging lens.

mcqs.q: What is the focal point (principal focus) of a lens, as explained using diagram A?
options: The mid point of the lens, denoted by O
The distance from the lens to the screen
The point where light rays meet after refraction through the lens
A line through the centre of curvature
mcqs.why: The focal point is the point where light rays meet after refraction through the lens, denoted by F; in diagram A parallel rays converge and meet at this point on the principal axis.

mcqs.q: What happens to the pupil of the eye in the dark?
options: It grows larger to let in more light
It stays closed by the shutter
mcqs.why: The iris controls the pupil size: the pupil grows larger to see things in the dark, whereas it contracts in bright light.

mcqs.q: In short sightedness, where are parallel rays focused by the eye lens?
mcqs.why: In short sightedness the eye lens becomes thick and its focal length is reduced, so parallel rays are focused in front of the retina instead of on it.

mcqs.q: How is long sightedness removed using a lens?
options: By wearing spectacles with a concave lens
By wearing spectacles with a convex lens of suitable focal length
By moving the eye lens back and forth
mcqs.why: Long sightedness, in which near objects cannot be seen clearly, is removed by wearing spectacles having a convex lens of suitable focal length, which converges the rays so they focus on the retina.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Electromagnetic induction is the production of current in a coil by relative motion between a magnet and the coil.
  • In hydro power, potential energy of stored water becomes kinetic, then mechanical, and finally electrical energy.
  • A steady wind of about 20 km/hr is needed for electricity generation from a wind mill.
  • Resistance is measured in ohms and capacitance is measured in farad (F).
  • A diode lets current flow in only one direction through its anode and cathode.
  • A rectifier converts AC to DC, while DC flows in one direction and AC changes its direction.
  • Main hydroelectric stations in Pakistan are at Tarbela, Mangla, Warsak and Ghazi Barotha.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Define electromagnetic induction.

Ans: When there is a relative motion between a magnet and a coil of wire, electric current starts flowing in the coil. This phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction. The direction of this current depends upon the direction of the relative motion between the magnet and the coil. The AC generator works on this principle.

Q: 2. Give few problems in generating electricity.

Ans: The book lists these problems: (1) Due to a prolonged period of low rainfall, the amount of water used for hydro power generation is of great concern. (2) The high cost of construction of dams and non-availability of suitable place for their construction. (3) Nuclear power plants have harmful effects on the nearby population and aquatic life due to nuclear radiations and wastes. (4) High cost of solar panels and storage batteries. (5) Steam-cycle plants require a great deal of water for cooling. (6) Generating electricity by wind mills requires high cost and a suitable place. (7) Electrical energy cannot be stored; it has to be converted to a different form. (8) Shortage of non-renewable energy sources like fossil fuels (coal, gas, oils). (9) Generating electricity causes noise, air and soil pollution at the point of generation.

Q: 3. How electricity is produced in hydro power stations?

Ans: Water is stored in an artificially made lake or reservoir at a certain height from sea level. When water is released from the reservoir, it flows down with speed through a turbine and turns its blades. The turning blades of the turbine in turn rotate the shaft of the generator, which generates electricity. In this way the potential energy of the stored water changes into kinetic energy, the kinetic energy of flowing water is converted into mechanical energy of the turbine, and finally this mechanical energy is converted into electrical energy by the generator. In Pakistan, the main hydroelectric power stations are at Tarbela, Mangla, Warsak and Ghazi Barotha.

Q: 4. What should be the speed of wind for the production of electricity from a wind mill?

Ans: A steady wind with a speed of about 20 km/hr is needed for the generation of electricity from a wind mill. The kinetic energy of the wind is converted into mechanical energy of the wind turbine, and the turbine in turn rotates the shaft of the connected generator to generate electrical energy. Because such a steady wind is not available everywhere, this method cannot be used everywhere.

Q: 5. Define the following terms: resistors, capacitors, diode, transistors and integrated circuit (IC).

Ans: Resistor: A resistor is a component that resists the flow of current. Resistance is measured in units called ohms and is denoted by the symbol (Ω). Capacitor: A capacitor is a device that can temporarily store an electric charge. Capacitance of a capacitor is measured in farad and is denoted by 'F'. Diode: A diode is a device that lets current flow in only one direction. It has two terminals, called the anode and the cathode; current flows only when positive voltage is applied to the anode and negative voltage to the cathode. Transistor: A transistor is a device with three terminals. Transistors are used as switches and amplifiers in electronic systems. Integrated circuit (IC): An integrated circuit is a special device that contains an entire electronic circuit, in which transistors, diodes and other elements are photographically engraved onto a tiny chip of silicon. Integrated circuits are the building blocks of modern electronic devices such as computers and cell phones.

Q: 6. How electricity can be generated in daily life?

Ans: In daily life, electricity can be generated by the methods described in this unit. A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction, for example the bicycle dynamo, which is a small generator attached to a bicycle: the top of the dynamo touches the tyre's rim and spins when the bicycle moves, and its coil spinning in a magnetic field produces current for the bicycle lamp. A battery (dry cell) generates electricity chemically, as used in torches and flash lights. Solar cells also generate electricity in daily use: when sunlight strikes a solar cell, it develops a voltage, and solar panels made of many solar cells generate electricity on a larger scale. On the large scale, electricity for our homes is generated in power stations from hydro, wind, nuclear, thermal and solar sources.

Q: 7. Make a list of sources of energy and explain any two in detail.

Ans: List of sources of electricity given in the unit: 1. The Battery, 2. Hydroelectric Power, 3. Wind Power, 4. Nuclear Power, 5. Thermal Power, 6. Solar Power. Tidal and geothermal energies can also be used to produce electricity. Two in detail: (1) Hydroelectric Power: The electricity generated by conversion of kinetic energy of water is called hydroelectric power. It is the cheapest and major source of electricity in Pakistan. Water stored in a reservoir at a height flows down, turns the blades of a turbine, and the turbine rotates the shaft of the generator to produce electricity. The main stations in Pakistan are at Tarbela, Mangla, Warsak and Ghazi Barotha. (2) Thermal Power: Generating electricity by means of heat produced by burning of fossil fuels like coal, gas or oil in a thermal power station is called thermal power. The heat generated by the burning of fossil fuel is used to convert water into steam. This steam is then used to rotate the steam turbine, which in turn rotates the shaft of the connected generator to produce electricity.

Q: 8. Explain the direct circuit and alternating current. [Printed as 'direct circuit'; read as direct current — see notes]

Ans: Direct current (D.C): The current which flows only in one direction is called Direct current (D.C). It does not change its direction. Alternating current (A.C): The current which changes its direction is called Alternating current (A.C). It changes its direction every moment. Alternating current is the most efficient way to deliver electrical power, however most electronic devices need direct current to function, so AC is converted to DC for such devices.

Q: 9. Which device is used to convert AC to DC.

Ans: The electrical device that converts AC to DC is called a rectifier, also called an AC to DC converter. Basically, a diode is the device which converts AC to DC, because a diode allows current to flow in only one direction. The AC to DC converter is either a part of the device itself or a part of its power cord.

Q: 10. What will happen if we do not use convertor while using DC operated device into AC outlet.

Ans: Most electronic devices need direct current (DC) to function, while the AC outlet supplies alternating current (AC), which changes its direction. If a DC operated device is used in an AC outlet without a convertor, the device will not get the steady one-direction current it needs, so it will not function properly. That is why the book states: if you have built a DC operated device and wish to power it from an AC outlet, you must add an AC to DC converter.

Project Work

Q: 1. Project. Design and demonstrate the working of a power station and also list the types of energy being used in the power station.

Ans: Working of a power station: Electricity is generated in power stations. In most power stations, fossil fuels (coal, gas etc.) are burnt to produce steam, and steam is used to turn the turbine. Electrical energy generation using steam turbines involves three energy conversions: (i) Extracting thermal energy from the fuel and using it to raise steam. (ii) Converting the thermal energy of the steam into kinetic energy in the turbine. (iii) Using a rotary generator to convert the turbine's mechanical energy into electrical energy. Types of energy used/converted in the power station: thermal (heat) energy of the fuel, thermal energy of steam, kinetic/mechanical energy of the turbine, and electrical energy produced by the generator. Diagram (in words): The printed figure shows a nuclear power station. On the left, inside the Containment building, is the Reactor vessel containing Uranium fuel and Control rods, connected to the Steam generators. Steam lines carry steam from the steam generators to the Turbine. The Turbine is coupled to the Generator, which is connected to the Transformer, and from the transformer Electricity is sent out on transmission lines/pylons on the right. Below the turbine is the Condenser, connected to Cooling water and a Pump. On the right stands the Cooling tower, with Warm water inlet at its top, Water vapor rising from its top, a Pump and Cold water basin at its base, and a Cool water source below it. Water circulates between the condenser, the pump, the cooling tower basin and the cool water source to cool the steam back into water.

lessons.title: Short Answers and Constructed Response Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A radio telescope's dish collects and focuses radio signals, the receiver converts them to electrical signals, and the analyzer creates an image.
  • Spectroscopes split white light into colours and help analyze materials that make up stars and nebulae.
  • Spacecraft are broadly classified into Robotic Space Crafts and Manned Space Crafts.
  • The Hubble Space telescope is a reflecting telescope launched in 1990, orbiting Earth at a height of 600 Km.
  • Without a space suit, man cannot live in space more than 2-3 minutes.
  • Solar cells were originally developed to provide electricity to space crafts and are now a source of clean electricity.
  • Space rockets, rocket launching pads and telecommunication systems are technologies used for space exploration.

Solved Exercises

Q: 1. Write the names of different parts of the radio telescope and their functions?

Ans: A radio telescope has several main parts: (1) Dish: The dish collects the radio signals from space and focuses them on the antenna. (2) Receiver: The receiver takes the radio waves received by the antenna and converts them to electrical signals (voltages). (3) Detector: The detector measures the power density of the electrical signal, which is necessary to turn the signals into a photo. (4) Analyzer: The analyzer, usually a computer or a device attached to a computer, takes the data and creates an image from it. Radio telescopes can receive signals during cloud cover, in the daytime as well as at night.

Q: 2. Write any three applications of space technology on earth.

Ans: Any three applications given in the unit are: (1) Metallic alloys: In order to withstand high temperatures and pressure, special types of metallic alloys have been developed for space craft, which are now used in jet engines. (2) Solar cells: Solar cells are now-a-days a source of free and clean electricity; these were originally developed to provide electricity to space crafts. (3) Liquid cooled garments: Liquid cooled garments manufactured for astronauts are currently used by car racers and nuclear reactor workers. (4) Anti-corrosion coatings: Anti corrosion coatings made for space crafts are now used on statues, bridges, pipelines etc. (Any three of these are the answer.)

Q: 3. What are the uses of spectroscope?

Ans: Spectroscopes are used in telescopes to help scientists in analyzing the materials that make up stars and nebulae. A spectroscope is an instrument used to examine different wavelengths (colours) of light; it splits white light into colours. With the help of spectroscopes, rays coming from distant objects are analyzed, and many characteristics of the body, including structure, chemical formation, speed of movement etc., are determined from this analysis. Every space probe is fitted with spectroscopes.

Q: 4. Enlist the problems faced by astronauts in space.

Ans: In space there are severe conditions which an astronaut has to face, for example very high temperature, zero gravity and zero pressure, which badly affect the human body; without a space suit, man cannot live in space more than 2-3 minutes. The problems resulting from space exploration listed in the unit are: (a) Weightlessness — when space craft enter the Earth's atmosphere their weight increases, which can damage the human body. (b) High temperatures, managed by liquid-cooled garments. (c) Corrosion of equipments, avoided by anti-corrosion coatings. (d) High cost of space programs.

Q: 5. Name the technologies used for space exploration.

Ans: Space exploration has become easy and result oriented with the help of the following technologies: (a) Space Rockets — space rockets are used for the transportation of space shuttle, space stations and other space crafts into space. (b) Rocket Launching Pads — these are especially built platforms for firing rockets into space, and they can withstand extremely high temperature. (c) Telecommunication system — special telecommunication systems are provided to rockets and space crafts to help the space crew communicate with each other and with the earth stations.

Q: 6. Write a detailed note on types of telescope.

Ans: The name 'telescope' covers a wide range of instruments. With respect to the radiations they detect, telescopes are of three types: (a) Optical telescope: An optical telescope gathers and focuses radiations mainly from the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum (called visible light). It increases the apparent angular size of distant objects as well as their apparent brightness, and helps photographers, star gazers and astronomers to spot the details of a distant object. Optical telescopes are of three kinds: (i) Refractor Telescope, which uses lenses; (ii) Reflector Telescope, which uses mirrors; (iii) Catadioptric Telescope, which uses mirrors with a lens design. The Hubble Space telescope is the reflecting telescope launched in 1990; it orbits around the Earth at a height of 600 Km and sends clear pictures of galaxies and other celestial bodies. (b) Radio telescope: A radio telescope is more sensitive and is able to create a visual picture of the signals it receives, not in visible light but in radio waves. This is extremely useful because there are objects that cannot be seen through visible light but can be seen by radio telescopes. Its main parts are a dish antenna, a receiver, a detector and an analyzer, and it can receive signals during cloud cover, in the daytime as well as at night. (c) Broad-spectrum telescope: Earth's atmosphere blocks out different rays coming from planets, stars and other heavenly bodies, so astronomers use telescopes into space to measure ultraviolet, infrared, gamma and X-rays as well as visible light and radio waves coming from outer space.

Q: 7. Explain the benefits of space exploration in detail.

Ans: Space technology has provided many benefits in our everyday life. Scientists invent products and techniques to meet the requirements of space exploration, and often these inventions can also be used on Earth: (i) Fire Fighting Equipment: Apollo technology has been used to produce a lighter breathing system for fire-fighters; the new system weighs about 9 kg and has a mask with greater peripheral vision. (ii) Firefighting Strategy: European Space Agency satellites provide information on fire locations, used to help develop fire fighting strategy. (iii) Vision Research: Landsat and Skylab technology is used to check the human eye for refractive error and cornea or lens obstruction. (iv) Global Positioning Satellites: Satellites orbiting the Earth, Earth monitoring stations and navigation receivers provide accurate positioning of ships, ground vehicles, airplanes and other portable devices; this technology has both military and non-military uses. (v) Cordless tools: The cordless tool was developed for the study of moon's soil samples; this technology is now used in the operating room, building construction, secret places and gardening. (vi) Active Pixel Sensor: This improved image technology requires less power, is less expensive and smaller than previous technology, and has provided better image for camcorders, digital cameras, night vision and x-rays. (vii) Tsunami Tracking: A satellite circling the Earth receives transmissions from under sea detectors and provides accurate information on tsunami size and strength. (viii) Archaeology: Space shuttle radar images help to locate ancient cities, roads and ruins, and helped to locate the lost city of Ubar in Oman. Special technology developed for space is also used to improve quality of life in health and medicine, global navigation, weather forecast and prediction of natural calamities, electronics and computers, and locating minerals, fossil fuels and water reserves.

Q: 8. Why spacecraft is used?

Ans: A spacecraft is a vehicle designed for space flights, also known as 'Space Ships'. Spacecraft are used for a variety of purposes including communications, earth observation, meteorology, navigation, planetary exploration and space tourism. Robotic space crafts are sent into space for collection of data about space, planets and other celestial bodies, while manned space crafts carry equipments along with humans to space.

Q: 9. In how many categories, spacecrafts are broadly classified.

Ans: Space Craft are broadly classified into two categories: (a) Robotic Space Crafts, and (b) Manned Space Crafts.

Q: 10. Differentiate between the categories of spacecrafts with examples.

Ans: Robotic Space Crafts: These are sent into space for collection of data about space, planets and other celestial bodies. They are controlled from the centre on earth, as they do not carry humans in them. Example: space probes — a space probe is a robotic spacecraft that travels through space to collect scientific information and does not orbit the earth; Voyager-1 and Voyager-2 were probes used for collecting data about Mars and Jupiter. Manned Space Crafts: These carry equipments along with humans to space. They contain all the facilities necessary for human survival such as oxygen, food, water and specially built cabins. Examples: space shuttle, which is a manned space craft sent into space with the help of a rocket and which returns and lands back on Earth like an aeroplane; and space stations, which are spacecraft capable of supporting a crew and designed to remain in space for a long time.

mcqs.q: In a radio telescope, what is the function of the dish?

It collects radio signals from space and focuses them on the antenna
It creates an image from the data
It converts radio waves to electrical signals
mcqs.why: The dish of a radio telescope collects the radio signals from space and focuses them on the antenna.

mcqs.q: In a radio telescope, the receiver does what?
options: Takes radio waves received by the antenna and converts them to electrical signals (voltages)

mcqs.q: What does a spectroscope do, as used in telescopes?
options: It splits white light into colours and examines different wavelengths of light
It collects radio signals from space
It measures wind speed in space
mcqs.why: A spectroscope examines different wavelengths (colours) of light and splits white light into colours, helping analyze materials in stars and nebulae.

mcqs.q: Spacecraft are broadly classified into which two categories?
options: Robotic Space Crafts and Manned Space Crafts
mcqs.why: Space Craft are broadly classified into two categories: Robotic Space Crafts and Manned Space Crafts.

options: Carrying humans with oxygen and food
Collection of data about space, planets and other celestial bodies
Landing back on Earth like an aeroplane
Supporting a crew for a long time
mcqs.why: Robotic Space Crafts are sent into space for collection of data about space, planets and other celestial bodies, and do not carry humans.

mcqs.q: The Hubble Space telescope is which kind of telescope, and when was it launched?
mcqs.why: The Hubble Space telescope is the reflecting telescope launched in 1990; it orbits around the Earth at a height of 600 Km.

options: The visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum (visible light)
mcqs.why: An optical telescope gathers and focuses radiations mainly from the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum, called visible light.

mcqs.q: According to the unit, without a space suit, how long can man live in space?
mcqs.why: In space there are severe conditions like very high temperature, zero gravity and zero pressure; without a space suit, man cannot live in space more than 2-3 minutes.
